name: Quadriceps contusion and myositis ossificans
populations: people with a previous quadriceps injury
summary: A direct blow that bleeds into the quadriceps, graded by knee flexion at 12–24 hours. Early knee flexion limits bleeding. Myositis ossificans and, rarely, compartment syndrome are the main complications.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean disability 13, 19 and 21 days for mild, moderate and severe contusions in 117 West Point cadets; mean lay-off 7 days for direct thigh injuries in elite football

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: When pain-free knee flexion and quadriceps size and firmness equal the other side. After immediate flexion to 120° for 24 hours, 47 midshipmen returned at a mean of 3.5 days (uncontrolled series)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Passive knee flexion at 12–24 hours: mild above 90°, moderate 45–90°, severe below 45°

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Often none is needed. Use ultrasound or MRI to define the haematoma, and radiographs or CT if a firm mass or lost flexion persists, for myositis ossificans

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young, active contact-sport athletes. The main series are cadets and midshipmen; direct injuries were 12% of thigh muscle injuries in elite football

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Direct thigh muscle injuries: 0.19 per 1,000 hours in elite football, against 1.48 for indirect injuries. Myositis ossificans developed in 9% of cadets with contusions

overview:
A quadriceps contusion is a muscle injury caused by a direct blunt force that crushes the muscle against the femur. Muscle contusion is second only to strain as a cause of sports-related morbidity, and severity depends on the site of impact, the activation status of the muscle, the age of the patient and fatigue [r1]. The injury consists of microscopic rupture of muscle cells, macroscopic defects in the muscle belly, infiltrative bleeding and inflammation, and repair is a race between remodelling and scar formation [r2]. In elite football, direct injuries made up 12% of 2,003 analysed thigh muscle injuries and caused a mean lay-off of 7 days against 18.5 days for indirect injuries [r3].

Severity is graded by passive knee flexion 12–24 hours after injury: in the West Point cohort, mild was above 90°, moderate 45–90° and severe below 45°, a grading that follows Jackson and Feagin [r4,r5]. The early flexed-knee approach holds the knee at 120° of flexion for 24 hours. In 47 midshipmen treated this way, the mean return to unrestricted activity was 3.5 days, and 1 of the first 23 had myositis ossificans on later radiographs [r6]. This was an uncontrolled descriptive series, so the benefit is not proven [r6].

The main complications are myositis ossificans (9% in 117 cadets) [r5] and, rarely, acute compartment syndrome, which has been reported in case reports [r7,r8,r9]. Advice on early treatment is contested. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may harm healing if used beyond 48 to 72 hours and corticosteroids are best avoided [r10], and conclusions about massage for severe muscle injury cannot yet be made [r11].

epidemiology.text: In 30 elite football teams followed from 2001 to 2013, 12% of 2,003 analysed thigh muscle injuries were direct (contusion), and the incidence of direct injuries was 0.19 per 1,000 hours against 1.48 for indirect injuries. The mean lay-off for direct injuries was 7 days, 76% occurred in matches, and foul play was involved in 42% of direct injuries [r3]. A 3-year study of 117 quadriceps contusions in West Point cadets found myositis ossificans in 9% [r5], and a prospective series of 47 midshipmen contusions was collected over 18 years [r6]. In 100 injured rugby players, six clinical tests were used to predict recovery time [r12]. Muscle contusion is second only to strain as a cause of sports-related morbidity [r1]. True population incidence outside these sporting and military groups was not identified.

intrinsic: Young age and active sport: the main published series are of cadets and midshipmen [r5,r6]
Severity depends on the activation status of the muscle, the age of the patient and fatigue [r1]
A previous quadriceps injury, which is a risk factor for myositis ossificans after contusion [r5]
extrinsic: Contact and collision sport: 76% of direct thigh injuries in elite football occurred in matches, and foul play was involved in 42% [r3]
Delay in treatment of more than 3 days, and playing football, were risk factors for myositis ossificans (delay is modifiable) [r5]
Whether the player could play on after the injury and the delay before treatment began were among the variables that predicted time to return in rugby players [r12]
Lack of thigh protection in contact sport (clinical reasoning; no study identified)

mechanism.summary: A contusion follows a direct blunt force to the front or side of the thigh, typically a knee, shoulder, helmet or boot in collision sport, which crushes the quadriceps against the femur. Severity depends on the site of impact, the activation status of the muscle, the age of the patient and fatigue [r1]. The injury is a sequence of microscopic rupture of muscle cells, macroscopic defects in the muscle belly, infiltrative bleeding and inflammation [r2]. The vastus intermedius and vastus lateralis lie closest to the bone, and the knee loses flexion because the swollen, bleeding quadriceps cannot lengthen [r5].
sequence: A player is struck on the anterior or anterolateral thigh, often by an opponent's knee in a collision or a tackle (clinical description).
The force compresses the quadriceps against the femoral shaft, so muscle fibres and their capillaries are crushed [r1,r2].
Torn vessels bleed into the muscle, forming an intramuscular haematoma, and inflammation follows [r2].
The thigh becomes swollen, tender and firm, and the quadriceps spasms, so passive knee flexion is limited, which is the basis for grading [r5].
Bleeding and spasm continue over the first 24 hours unless the knee is held in flexion, which is the rationale for the 120° flexion position [r13].
In a few cases pressure inside the thigh compartment rises and causes progressive pain at rest (acute compartment syndrome) [r7].
As the muscle repairs, regeneration competes with scar formation, and in some cases bone forms inside the haematoma (myositis ossificans) [r2,r5].

variants.name: Mild, moderate and severe contusion
variants.description: Graded by passive knee flexion 12–24 hours after injury: mild above 90°, moderate 45–90°, severe below 45° in the West Point cohort [r5].

variants.name: Contusion with myositis ossificans
variants.description: Myositis ossificans developed in 9% of 117 cadets, and it was linked to knee motion below 120°, football, a previous quadriceps injury, delayed treatment of more than 3 days and an ipsilateral knee effusion [r5].

variants.name: Contusion progressing to acute compartment syndrome
variants.description: Case reports describe athletes with progressive pain after a thigh contusion who needed fasciotomy; one 17-year-old footballer returned to play at 4 months [r7,r8,r9].

variants.name: Closed degloving (Morel-Lavallée) lesion mistaken for a contusion
variants.description: A case report describes a massive medial knee and thigh Morel-Lavallée lesion initially diagnosed as a quadriceps contusion, with delayed treatment and recurrence [r14].

variants.name: Repeat contusion
variants.description: A previous quadriceps injury was a risk factor for myositis ossificans [r5], so protect an injured thigh from a repeat blow until flexion and strength have returned (clinical reasoning).

anatomy.text: The quadriceps lies on the front and sides of the femur. The rectus femoris is superficial and central, the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis lie to either side, and the vastus intermedius lies deepest, directly on the femoral shaft (standard anatomy). The muscles are enclosed by the fascia lata, and the femoral nerve and artery run in the anteromedial thigh. Knee flexion requires the quadriceps to lengthen, so a haematoma and spasm in the muscle limit flexion, which is why range of motion measures the severity of a contusion [r5]. The anterolateral thigh is the most common contusion site in collision sport (clinical teaching).

structures.name: Vastus lateralis
structures.role: Lateral quadriceps head, exposed to the commonest anterolateral impact. Extends the knee

structures.name: Vastus intermedius
structures.role: Deepest quadriceps muscle on the femoral shaft, so it is crushed against bone in a direct blow. Extends the knee

structures.name: Rectus femoris
structures.role: Superficial, biarticular quadriceps head that extends the knee and flexes the hip

structures.name: Vastus medialis
structures.role: Medial head. It extends the knee and stabilises the patella

structures.name: Fascia lata and anterior thigh compartment
structures.role: Fibrous envelope around the quadriceps. A large haematoma inside it can raise pressure and cause compartment syndrome [r7]

structures.name: Femoral nerve and artery
structures.role: Neurovascular bundle in the anteromedial thigh. Check it when there is a tense, painful thigh [r9]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
A contusion is crush injury. It consists of microscopic rupture and damage to muscle cells, macroscopic defects in the muscle belly, infiltrative bleeding and inflammation, and repair can be thought of as a race between remodelling and scar formation [r2]. Bleeding forms a haematoma within the quadriceps, and swelling and spasm restrict knee flexion, which grades severity [r5]. On ultrasound, hyperechoic and hypoechoic lesions differ in prognosis: in a 7-patient series, contusions with hyperechoic lesions returned earlier than those with hypoechoic findings, and clinical grading did not consistently estimate return to play [r15]. NSAIDs modestly inhibit the initial inflammatory response, but may have small negative effects later in healing [r16], and evidence suggests a negative influence on muscle satellite cells [r17].

Two complications matter. Myositis ossificans is a self-limiting, benign ossifying lesion within soft tissue, most often within muscle [r18]. It developed in 9% of 117 cadets with contusions, linked to knee motion below 120°, football, a previous quadriceps injury, treatment delay of more than 3 days and an ipsilateral knee effusion [r5]. Imaging evolves with time and shows a zonal pattern and peripheral maturation, and early findings can mimic a sarcoma [r19,r18]. Acute compartment syndrome is much rarer. High intramuscular pressure with a major haematoma caused severe pain at rest after blunt trauma in two athletes who needed fasciotomy [r7].

structures.name: Quadriceps muscle belly (vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, rectus femoris)
structures.effect: Crushed against the femur, with torn fibres and a haematoma within the muscle [r2]

structures.name: Intramuscular haematoma
structures.effect: Blood collects in the muscle. On ultrasound, hypoechoic lesions were associated with slower return to play than hyperechoic lesions in a small series [r15]

structures.name: Fascia lata and thigh compartment
structures.effect: A large haematoma can raise compartment pressure and cause compartment syndrome in a minority [r7,r9]

structures.name: Heterotopic bone (myositis ossificans)
structures.effect: Bone forms within the haematoma in some cases, with a zonal maturation pattern on imaging [r19,r5]

structures.name: Femoral periosteum and bone
structures.effect: The femur takes the force against the crushed muscle, so check for a femoral fracture if pain is severe or localised to bone (clinical convention)

muscles.name: Quadriceps (vastus intermedius and lateralis most often)
muscles.effect: Pain, spasm and haematoma restrict lengthening, so passive knee flexion falls [r5]. Quadriceps size and firmness should return to equal the other side [r6].

muscles.name: Hip flexors (rectus femoris) and hamstrings
muscles.effect: These muscles compensate for the quadriceps during gait and sport (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Hip abductors and calf
muscles.effect: The kinetic chain adapts to a stiff or painful knee and can overload other tissues if the limp persists (clinical reasoning).

cellular.description: The crush ruptures myofibres and capillaries, and a haematoma forms in the muscle [r2].
Neutrophils and macrophages clear necrotic tissue. Anti-inflammatory drugs modestly reduce the early response but may harm later healing [r16,r17].
Satellite cells proliferate and form new fibres while fibroblasts lay down scar. Repair is a race between remodelling and scar formation [r2].
The scar remodels along the line of load. In some patients bone forms within the haematoma, and follow-up radiographs were taken at 3 and 6 months in the midshipmen series [r6].

systems.effect: A large haematoma, and rarely raised compartment pressure that compromises perfusion [r7]. Anticoagulant use or a bleeding disorder worsens bleeding (clinical reasoning).
Pain, spasm and reflex quadriceps inhibition restrict movement. Femoral nerve function should be checked if the thigh is tense or the pain progresses [r9].
Early inflammation clears debris, and NSAIDs modestly reduce it with possible negative effects later in healing [r16]. Satellite cells may be affected [r17].
A limp and stiff knee shift load to the hip, pelvis and other leg (clinical reasoning).
Fear of a repeat blow and of lost flexion affects return to contact sport, so progress should be criteria-based (clinical reasoning).

grading.system: Jackson–Feagin grading by passive knee flexion 12–24 hours after injury (thresholds as applied in the West Point cohort) [r4,r5]

grades.description: Knee flexion greater than 90° at 12–24 hours [r5].
grades.prognosis: Mean disability 13 days in 117 West Point cadets [r5]

grades.description: Knee flexion less than 45° at 12–24 hours [r5]. Check for compartment syndrome if pain is progressive [r7].
grades.prognosis: Mean disability 21 days [r5]. Grading did not consistently estimate return to play in a 7-patient ultrasound series, so reassess [r15].

timeframes.summary: Time off depends on severity. In 117 West Point cadets, mean disability was 13, 19 and 21 days for mild, moderate and severe contusions [r5]. In elite football, direct thigh injuries had a mean lay-off of 7 days [r3]. After immediate immobilisation in 120° of flexion, 47 midshipmen returned to unrestricted activity at a mean of 3.5 days (range 2–5), in an uncontrolled series [r6]. If myositis ossificans forms, recovery is longer: in 19 athletes, 89.5% resumed light activity 3 months after diagnosis and returned to their earlier level at 6 months [r20].

healing.description: Knee held in 120° of flexion for 24 hours to limit bleeding and preserve flexion [r6,r13]
Haematoma forms and inflammation clears debris (general muscle biology) [r2]
Satellite cell regeneration competes with scar formation; early pain-free flexion and strengthening begin [r2,r5]
Remodelling continues. Radiographs were repeated at 3 and 6 months in one series [r6]

milestones.label: Brace off after 24 hours in flexion
milestones.note: In the midshipmen protocol, active pain-free stretching and isometric strengthening then began [r6]

milestones.label: Return to unrestricted activity after immediate flexion (mean)
milestones.note: 3.5 days, range 2–5, in 47 midshipmen; an uncontrolled series [r6]

milestones.label: Mean lay-off for direct thigh injuries in elite football
Light activity after myositis ossificans diagnosis
Earlier level of sport after myositis ossificans

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. The goal is pain-free knee flexion and quadriceps size and firmness equal to the uninjured side [r6], and regaining 120° or more of flexion is the determining factor for safe return [r13]. Typical times in cohorts are 13, 19 and 21 days for mild, moderate and severe contusions [r5] and a mean lay-off of 7 days in elite football [r3]. If myositis ossificans forms, expect about 3 months to light activity and 6 months to the earlier level [r20]. These figures come from military and elite-football cohorts, so use them as a guide.

symptoms: Pain, swelling and a feeling of tightness in the front or side of the thigh after a direct blow [r1]
Inability to continue play after the impact, with stiffness developing over the next hours [r6]
Difficulty bending the knee and limping, especially on stairs and when getting up from a chair
Pain with a straight-leg raise or isometric quadriceps contraction in moderate and severe injuries [r6]
Pain that increases rather than settles, with a tense thigh: a warning sign of compartment syndrome [r7,r8]
signs: A firm, tender swelling over the anterior or anterolateral thigh, with bruising that may track distally
Reduced passive knee flexion on the injured side, which defines the grade [r5]
Thigh circumference greater than the other side and increased muscle firmness [r12]
Painful or weak active knee extension, and a limp
In compartment syndrome: tense swelling, severe pain with passive stretch, and possible neurovascular change [r7,r9]

subjective: Mechanism: a direct blow (knee, shoulder, helmet, boot), the site and the time of injury [r1]
Whether the player could continue after the impact: inability to continue was an inclusion criterion in the midshipmen series [r6]
Previous quadriceps injury and previous myositis ossificans, which are risk factors [r5]
Pain trajectory: pain that is rising, constant at rest or out of proportion needs urgent review for compartment syndrome [r7,r8]
Time since injury and what has been done so far, because delay in treatment of more than 3 days raised the risk of myositis ossificans [r5]
Medicines and conditions that increase bleeding: anticoagulants, antiplatelets or bleeding disorders (clinical convention)
Knee effusion, which was a risk factor for myositis ossificans [r5]
observation: Swelling and bruising of the thigh, and the position the leg is held in
Gait: limp, reduced knee flexion in swing, and avoidance of weight bearing
Thigh circumference compared with the other side [r12]
Skin integrity and the possibility of an open wound or a closed degloving injury [r14]
palpation: Muscle firmness (rated against the other side), with tenderness over the anterolateral thigh. Muscle firmness ratings and unilateral palpation, brush-swipe and tap tests had substantial to excellent reliability (0.66 to 1.00) in rugby players [r12]
Tension of the thigh and whether it is soft or tense (compartment screen) [r7]
Femoral shaft for bony tenderness, to exclude a fracture (clinical convention)
Distal pulses and capillary refill in a tense thigh [r9]
rangeOfMotion: Passive knee flexion (prone), measured with a goniometer and compared with the other side. Grade at 12–24 hours: mild above 90°, moderate 45–90°, severe below 45° [r5]
Regaining 120° or more of knee flexion is the determining factor for safe return [r13]
Knee extension, and hip flexion and extension, which can be limited by the rectus femoris
strength: Straight-leg raise and a pain-free isometric quadriceps contraction. Inability to do both was an inclusion criterion in the midshipmen series [r6]
Resisted knee extension and hip flexion, compared with the other side
Thigh girth and quadriceps firmness as indirect size measures [r12]
neuro: Femoral nerve screen: quadriceps power, patellar reflex and anterior thigh sensation, especially with a tense thigh [r9]
Distal neurovascular status in the foot (pulses, colour, sensation) in severe or progressive cases [r9]
functional: Gait, stairs, sit-to-stand and squat, compared with the other side
Single-leg squat and step-down control once pain allows
Running, hop and landing tasks before return to sport
Sport-specific tasks, including contact drills with protective padding

specialTests.name: Passive knee flexion range (prone) at 12–24 hours
specialTests.purpose: Grade the severity of the contusion
specialTests.procedure: With the person prone, flex the knee passively to the first firm resistance or pain limit and measure with a goniometer. Compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Mild: above 90°. Moderate: 45–90°. Severe: below 45°. These are the West Point thresholds. Clinical grading did not consistently estimate return to play in a 7-patient ultrasound series [r15]. No sensitivity or specificity was identified.

specialTests.name: Thigh circumference and muscle firmness
specialTests.procedure: Measure circumference at set points (for example the suprapatellar border) and rate firmness against the other side.
specialTests.positive: Greater circumference and firmness than the other side. In 100 rugby players, a regression using the difference in knee range, relative firmness, difference in circumference, being able to play on and delay before treatment explained 64% of the variance in time to return to full training [r12]. This is a prediction model and not diagnostic accuracy.

specialTests.name: Straight-leg raise with pain-free isometric quadriceps contraction
specialTests.purpose: Separate a contusion that blocks function from a mild one
specialTests.procedure: With the person supine, ask for a quadriceps contraction and a straight-leg raise with the knee locked in full extension.
specialTests.positive: Inability to perform both, or pain, was used to define injuries that could not continue play in the midshipmen series [r6]. No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Compartment screen
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the thigh for tension, test pain with passive knee flexion (stretch), check pulses and sensation, and recheck over hours. If suspected, arrange urgent compartment pressure measurement per local protocol.
specialTests.positive: Progressive pain at rest after blunt trauma should raise suspicion [r7]. In one case, measured compartment pressure confirmed the diagnosis [r9]. No accuracy figures were identified.

clinicalRules.name: Grading by knee flexion
clinicalRules.description: Grade the contusion by passive knee flexion at 12–24 hours: mild above 90°, moderate 45–90°, severe below 45° [r5]. Reassess, because clinical grading did not always estimate return to play [r15].

clinicalRules.name: Progressive pain after blunt trauma
clinicalRules.description: A compartment syndrome with a major haematoma should be considered as a cause of progressive pain at rest after blunt muscle trauma [r7]. No validated clinical rule was identified.

outcomeMeasures.name: Passive knee flexion (goniometer)
outcomeMeasures.use: The grading and progression measure; 120° or more is the determining factor for safe return [r13]

outcomeMeasures.name: Thigh circumference and muscle firmness rating
outcomeMeasures.use: Track swelling and recovery. Both are part of a model that predicted recovery time in rugby players [r12]

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain numerical rating scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain at rest, on stairs and in sport tasks (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Quadriceps strength (limb symmetry index)
outcomeMeasures.use: Isometric or isokinetic strength compared with the other side (clinical convention). Quadriceps size and firmness should equal the other side before return [r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Return-to-sport status and time lost
outcomeMeasures.use: Days to unrestricted activity, for comparison with cohorts: 13, 19 and 21 days by grade in West Point cadets [r5]

imaging.indication: To exclude a femoral fracture after a severe blow, and to look for myositis ossificans when pain, a firm mass or lost flexion persists beyond the expected course
imaging.findings: Normal early. Ossification appears later: in the midshipmen series, radiographs at 3 and 6 months in 23 men showed 1 case of myositis ossificans [r6]. Imaging evolves with a zonal pattern and peripheral maturation [r19].

imaging.indication: To define the extent of the haematoma, to guide monitoring and to look for early myositis ossificans
imaging.findings: In a 7-patient series, hyperechoic lesions returned earlier than hypoechoic ones, and hypoechoic lesions may need closer monitoring [r15]. Ultrasound can also exclude a Morel-Lavallée lesion [r14].

imaging.indication: For an atypical or persistent mass, when the diagnosis is unclear, or to rule out a tumour
imaging.findings: Early myositis ossificans can mimic a soft-tissue sarcoma on imaging, and a biopsy may be needed if imaging is indeterminate [r18,r19]. MRI also helps to identify extensive haematoma or a closed degloving injury [r14,r21].

differentials.name: Quadriceps strain
differentials.distinguishing: Indirect injury without a blow, from sprinting or kicking, with pain in the muscle belly and the central tendon, and a sharper loss of function with resisted extension. A contusion follows a direct blow.

differentials.name: Quadriceps tendon rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Inability to extend the knee against gravity, a suprapatellar gap and a patella that sits low, usually in older people or those with tendon disease.

differentials.name: Acute compartment syndrome of the thigh
differentials.distinguishing: Progressive pain at rest after blunt trauma, a tense thigh, pain with passive stretch and neurovascular change. It is rare and needs urgent pressure measurement [r7,r9].

differentials.name: Femoral shaft fracture or stress injury
differentials.distinguishing: Bony tenderness, deformity or inability to bear weight after high-energy trauma, or a rise in load and night pain, with a fracture on radiograph or MRI.

differentials.name: Morel-Lavallée lesion (closed degloving injury)
differentials.distinguishing: A large fluctuant collection above the fascia after a shearing injury, which recurs after aspiration. It was misdiagnosed as a contusion in a case report [r14].

differentials.name: Myositis ossificans versus a soft-tissue sarcoma
differentials.distinguishing: A persistent or growing mass after a blow. Imaging in myositis ossificans shows a zonal pattern with peripheral maturation, whereas a sarcoma does not; biopsy may be needed if imaging is indeterminate [r19,r18].

differentials.name: Iliac crest contusion (hip pointer)
differentials.distinguishing: Direct blow to the iliac crest, with tenderness at the pelvic rim and pain on trunk side bending, not over the quadriceps.

redFlags: Pain that is increasing, constant at rest or out of proportion to the injury, a tense thigh, or pain with passive stretch: suspect acute compartment syndrome. Send to the emergency department the same day for compartment pressure measurement and surgical review [r7,r9,r8].
Pale, cold or numb foot, absent pulses or new femoral nerve weakness: refer as an emergency for vascular and neurological assessment [r9].
Inability to bear weight, deformity or severe localised bone tenderness after high-energy trauma: exclude a femoral fracture with a radiograph.
Anticoagulant use, a bleeding disorder, or a rapidly enlarging haematoma: arrange urgent medical review, and do not massage or stretch the thigh (clinical convention).

A firm mass, persistent pain or loss of knee flexion beyond the expected course, or night pain and weight loss: image for myositis ossificans, a Morel-Lavallée lesion or a tumour, and refer for review [r18,r14,r5].
Fever, spreading redness or a wound over the haematoma: suspect infection and refer the same day.

management.principles: Treat a thigh contusion as a bleeding injury in the first 24 hours, then restore flexion early and strengthen by criteria. Start with the knee in 120° of flexion for 24 hours [r10,r6], then pain-free active flexion exercises and isometric strengthening, advancing activity as range returns [r10,r6]. Check carefully for progressive pain, a tense thigh and neurovascular change, because compartment syndrome is rare but serious [r7]. Be honest about the evidence: the flexed-knee protocol rests on uncontrolled military cohorts [r5,r6]. NSAIDs beyond 48 to 72 hours may harm healing and corticosteroids are best avoided [r10,r16], and conclusions about massage for severe muscle injury cannot yet be made [r11]. Most contusions recover in days to a few weeks, and myositis ossificans is usually managed conservatively with ultrasound monitoring [r5,r20].

medical.name: Immediate knee flexion to 120° for 24 hours
medical.description: On diagnosis, the knee is passively flexed painlessly to 120° and held continuously for 24 hours in a brace or wrap. In 47 midshipmen this was followed by return to unrestricted activity in a mean of 3.5 days, and 1 of the first 23 had myositis ossificans on radiographs [r6]. A 117-cadet study used rest in flexion instead of extension, with disability of 13, 19 and 21 days by grade [r5]. A review describes it as the start of treatment [r10]. The evidence is uncontrolled.

medical.name: Rest, ice and compression in the first 24–48 hours
medical.description: Described as the acute-phase treatment alongside a planned return-to-play protocol [r21]. Whether icing as usually practised cools muscle enough to influence repair is doubted [r11].

medical.name: Short course of NSAIDs (up to 48–72 hours)
medical.description: NSAIDs modestly inhibit the initial inflammatory response and its symptoms, but may have small negative effects later in healing [r16]. A review states that NSAIDs can be detrimental if used for more than 48 to 72 hours [r10]. Any early benefit may not persist, and satellite cells may be harmed [r17]. No source reviewed tested NSAIDs for preventing myositis ossificans after quadriceps contusion.

medical.name: Prolonged NSAID use (beyond 48–72 hours)
medical.description: Can be detrimental to healing according to a review of thigh contusion [r10], and an overview found a possible deficit in long-term repair [r17].

medical.name: Corticosteroid injection into the contused muscle
medical.description: Corticosteroids should be avoided according to a review of thigh contusion [r10], and they have generally been shown to adversely affect healing of acute muscle injuries [r16].

medical.name: Emergency fasciotomy with haematoma evacuation for acute compartment syndrome
medical.description: Reported in two athletes with a contusion and compartment syndrome [r7], in a 17-year-old footballer who returned to play at 4 months [r8], and in a 19-year-old footballer after compartment pressure measurement [r9]. All are case reports.

medical.name: Conservative management of myositis ossificans with ultrasound monitoring
medical.description: In a series of 19 athletes, therapeutic abstention and persistence of ossification did not seem to prevent return to the earlier level, with ultrasound monitoring; 89.5% resumed light activity at 3 months [r20].

medical.name: Surgical excision of mature, symptomatic myositis ossificans
medical.description: Treatment is complex and often multidisciplinary, and diagnosis must be secure because imaging can mimic a tumour [r18]. Reserve excision for a mature lesion that causes persistent pain or loss of motion (clinical convention).

physio.name: Early recognition, grading and serial reassessment
physio.description: Grade by passive knee flexion at 12–24 hours and reassess daily, and screen for compartment syndrome [r5,r7]. Variables such as the difference in knee range, firmness and circumference help predict recovery time [r12].

physio.name: Early pain-free active quadriceps stretching and isometric strengthening after the first 24 hours
physio.description: After 24 hours in flexion, the midshipmen performed active, pain-free quadriceps stretching several times a day and pain-free isometric quadriceps strengthening as soon as possible. The goals were pain-free knee flexion and quadriceps size and firmness equal to the uninjured side [r6].

physio.name: Staged program with early flexion exercises
physio.description: The West Point program emphasised early flexion exercises instead of extension exercises, within a three-phase therapy program, with return to full activity and normal knee motion as targets [r5]. A review recommends range-of-motion exercises and then advancement of activity [r10].

physio.name: Cryokinetics with modified training
physio.description: In 100 rugby players, a standardised program incorporating cryokinetics and modified training was used [r12]. The effect of each component cannot be separated.

physio.name: Early massage, deep heat and forceful passive stretching in the first days
physio.description: A traditional precaution against bleeding and myositis ossificans, but contested. Conclusions about massage for more severe muscle injury cannot yet be made because of a lack of experimental evidence [r11], and no source reviewed tested early heat or forceful stretching. Avoid them while the haematoma is evolving, as a precaution (expert opinion).

physio.name: Return to contact sport before flexion and strength recover
physio.description: Regaining 120° or more of knee flexion is the determining factor for safe return [r13], and a previous quadriceps injury raises the myositis ossificans risk [r5].

education: Keep the knee bent as advised for the first 24 hours. Bleeding into the muscle is what stiffens the knee, and the position helps keep your bend.
Do not rub, massage or heat the thigh in the first days, and do not take anti-inflammatory tablets for longer than 2 to 3 days unless your doctor says so.
Go to the emergency department at once if the pain keeps getting worse, the thigh feels tight, or your foot becomes cold, pale or numb.
Bend and strengthen the knee gently but regularly, as pain allows, and return to sport only when your bend and thigh strength match the other side.
Tell your clinician if a hard lump forms or your knee bend stops improving after a few weeks, because bone can form in the muscle (myositis ossificans).

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is criteria-based and is built on the flexion-first approach: 24 hours of knee flexion to 120°, then early active, pain-free flexion and isometric work, then strength and sport tasks [r6,r5,r10]. Time-based figures vary: mean disability was 13, 19 and 21 days by grade in West Point cadets [r5] and 3.5 days after immediate flexion in midshipmen [r6], and these were uncontrolled cohorts. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not from a single source. Keep exercise pain at or below about 3 to 4 out of 10, and settled within 24 hours (clinical convention). Treat progressive pain or a tense thigh as an emergency at any stage [r7].

stages.name: Flex and protect
goals: Limit bleeding and spasm and preserve knee flexion
Protect the thigh from a repeat blow
Screen for compartment syndrome and fracture
Start crutches if weight bearing is painful
precautions: Hold the knee in 120° of flexion for 24 hours only if it can be done painlessly [r6]
No massage, deep heat or forceful stretching in this phase (expert opinion) [r11]
Seek emergency review for rising pain, a tense thigh or neurovascular change [r7,r9]

exercises.name: Knee held in 120° of flexion (brace, wrap or sling)
exercises.dosage: Continuously for 24 hours, then remove as the protocol directs
exercises.cues: Flex the knee passively to 120° without pain, and stop if pain increases

exercises.name: Ankle pumps
exercises.dosage: 20 repetitions every hour while awake (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Smooth and complete range, which keeps the calf pump active

exercises.name: Protected walking with crutches
exercises.dosage: Short walks as needed, with weight shared through the crutches
exercises.cues: Even steps, with the injured knee as straight as comfortable

progressionCriteria: 24 hours of flexion completed with no rising pain or tense swelling
Resting pain controlled and the foot warm with normal sensation
No sign of compartment syndrome or fracture

stages.name: Restore flexion and activate
goals: Restore pain-free knee flexion toward 120° and equal to the other side
precautions: Pain-free active stretching only, with no forced passive stretching
No heat or deep massage while the haematoma is evolving [r11]
Reassess flexion daily and refer if it plateaus or a firm mass develops [r5]

exercises.name: Active heel slide (knee flexion)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10, several times daily within the pain-free range
exercises.cues: Slide the heel toward the buttock and aim to equal the other side

exercises.name: Gentle active quadriceps stretch
exercises.cues: Mild stretch only, with no sharp pain; the midshipmen protocol used active pain-free stretching [r6]

exercises.name: Quadriceps set
exercises.cues: Press the knee down and tighten the thigh gently

exercises.name: Straight-leg raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10, daily, once there is no lag
exercises.cues: Lock the knee and lift with the thigh muscle

exercises.name: Stationary cycling (low resistance)
exercises.cues: Raise the saddle so that knee flexion is easy and pain-free

progressionCriteria: Passive knee flexion at 120° or equal to the other side [r13]
Straight-leg raise with no lag and pain-free isometric contraction
No increase in swelling, firmness or pain after sessions

stages.name: Strength and function
goals: Regain quadriceps size and firmness equal to the other side [r6]
Restore squat, stair and step control
Strengthen the hip and hamstrings alongside the quadriceps
precautions: Progress load only if the previous session settled within 24 hours
Watch for a new firm mass or a plateau in flexion, which should prompt imaging for myositis ossificans [r5,r18]
Keep contact and impact out until flexion and strength have recovered

exercises.name: Bodyweight squat
exercises.cues: Weight through the whole foot, knees over the second toe

exercises.name: Step-up
exercises.cues: Control the knee over the second toe and keep the pelvis level

exercises.name: Forward lunge
exercises.cues: Torso upright, with the front knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels and keep the ribs down

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise
exercises.cues: Pause at the top

exercises.name: Single-leg balance
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee soft

progressionCriteria: Pain-free knee flexion equal to the other side
Thigh girth and firmness close to the other side [r6,r12]
Single-leg squat and step-down controlled with no knee collapse
No next-day swelling or pain after strength sessions

stages.name: Return to sport
stages.timeframe: Weeks 2–6+ (criteria-based; longer for severe injury or myositis ossificans)
goals: Change of direction and sport-specific drills
Padded contact drills before full contact
Quadriceps strength symmetry of about 90% or more
precautions: Add impact and contact stepwise (about 10–20% per week, clinical convention)
Use thigh padding in contact sport (clinical convention)
If myositis ossificans is confirmed, progress by pain, range and ultrasound findings, and expect about 3 months to light activity and 6 months to the earlier level [r20]

exercises.name: Walk-to-jog progression
exercises.dosage: Alternate 1–2 min jog and 1–2 min walk, building to continuous jogging over 1–2 weeks
exercises.cues: Quiet, even footfalls

exercises.name: Single-leg hop progressions
exercises.cues: Soft landing, stick for 2 s

exercises.name: Drop landing then rebound jump
exercises.cues: Land softly with hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change-of-direction drills
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sessions per week, progressing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Lower the centre of mass, with the knee over the foot

exercises.name: Padded contact drills
exercises.dosage: Start at low intensity, then build to full contact over 1–2 weeks
exercises.cues: Pad the thigh, and stop for pain or a loss of flexion

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance (squat, split squat)
exercises.cues: Keep the loads heavy and the tempo controlled

progressionCriteria: Completes full training for at least 1–2 weeks with no pain, swelling or loss of flexion
Knee flexion and quadriceps size and firmness equal to the other side [r6]
Strength and hop symmetry about 90% or more (clinical convention)
Clinician and athlete agree, with thigh protection in place for contact

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria for quadriceps contusion were identified in the sources reviewed; the criteria below reflect published goals and clinical convention
Pain-free knee flexion that equals the other side, with at least 120° [r13,r6]
Quadriceps size and firmness equal to the uninjured side, with no residual swelling [r6]
No tenderness, no firm mass and no loss of range after running and heavy training
Quadriceps strength and hop symmetry about 90% (clinical convention)
Tolerates graded sport and padded contact drills for at least 1–2 weeks without a flare. If myositis ossificans is present, ossification is stable and range is maintained [r20]
tests: Prone passive knee flexion compared with the other side
Thigh circumference and muscle firmness rating [r12]
Isometric or isokinetic quadriceps strength with limb symmetry index
Single-leg squat, step-down and hop tests
Ultrasound follow-up if there is any concern about myositis ossificans [r15,r20]

prognosis: Most contusions recover in days to weeks. In 117 West Point cadets, mean disability was 13, 19 and 21 days for mild, moderate and severe contusions, and myositis ossificans developed in 9% [r5]. After immediate flexion to 120°, 47 midshipmen returned in a mean of 3.5 days, with 1 of the first 23 showing myositis ossificans [r6]. In elite football, direct injuries kept players out for a mean of 7 days [r3]. When myositis ossificans forms, 89.5% of 19 athletes resumed light activity 3 months after diagnosis and returned to their earlier level at 6 months, and persisting ossification did not prevent return [r20]. Acute compartment syndrome is rare but serious, and in one case the player returned to play at 4 months after fasciotomy [r8]. These figures come from military and elite-football cohorts and uncontrolled series, so individual recovery varies.
prevention: Protective thigh padding in contact and collision sport (clinical reasoning; no prevention study was identified).
Treat promptly: delay in treatment of more than 3 days was a risk factor for myositis ossificans [r5].
Do not return to contact before full flexion and strength return, because a previous quadriceps injury raises the myositis ossificans risk [r5,r13].
Avoid early heat, deep massage and forceful stretching of the haematoma, as a precaution (expert opinion; the evidence is uncertain) [r11].
Check progressive pain early, since compartment syndrome needs urgent surgery [r7].
clinicalPearls: Grade at 12–24 hours, not at the pitch side: swelling and spasm evolve, and passive knee flexion at that time defines mild (above 90°), moderate (45–90°) and severe (below 45°) contusions [r5].
Regaining 120° or more of knee flexion is the determining factor for safe return, so measure it at every visit [r13].
The flexed-knee approach is attractive but rests on uncontrolled military cohorts. Explain it as a reasonable approach and not a proven cure [r6,r5].
Progressive pain at rest after a blunt thigh injury is compartment syndrome until proved otherwise. Do not treat it as a bad contusion [r7,r9].
Be cautious with NSAIDs beyond 48 to 72 hours and with corticosteroid injection, and be honest that massage has no good evidence in severe injury [r10,r11].

A mass that persists, firmness that does not soften or a flexion plateau should prompt imaging for myositis ossificans. Do not rush to biopsy, because early myositis ossificans can mimic a sarcoma [r18,r19].

forces.label: Direct blow to the front of the thigh

captions.text: A footballer runs with the ball while an opponent closes in at speed.
The opponent's knee drives into the front of his thigh.
The quadriceps is crushed against the femur: a direct blow, with no stretch involved.
He pulls up, grabs the thigh and finds it hard to bend the knee.
Swelling and stiffness build over the next hours.
Zooming into the front of the right thigh, viewed from the front.
The quadriceps lies on the femur: the vastus lateralis is on the side, the vastus intermedius is deepest.
A direct blow compresses the muscle against the bone.
Crushed fibres and torn capillaries bleed, forming an intramuscular haematoma.
The thigh swells and the muscle spasms, so the knee cannot bend fully.
Rarely, bleeding raises pressure in the thigh compartment, with progressive pain at rest.
In some patients, bone forms in the haematoma weeks later: myositis ossificans.
Early knee flexion, careful monitoring and graded loading guide recovery.
Healthy muscle: myofibres made of aligned sarcomeres.
A direct crush ruptures fibre membranes and disrupts the sarcomeres.
Torn capillaries bleed and a haematoma fills the defect.
Neutrophils and macrophages clear necrotic fibre debris.
Satellite cells activate and proliferate.
New myotubes form and fuse with surviving fibres.
A connective-tissue scar matures. Repair is a race between regeneration and scar, and graded loading helps alignment.
